title: In rare Monday playoff, Viktor Hovland beats Scottie Scheffler for Travelers Championship
content:
In front of a large crowd for a 9 a.m. Monday playoff for one hole to decide the Travelers Championship, Viktor Hovland took down World No. 1 Scottie Scheffler to restake his claim in the game.

All the better, he did it with a large faction of Norwegian fans in tow, after they detoured to Cromwell, Conn., from Boston following Norway’s World Cup match Friday.

Scheffler missed a short birdie putt that would have extended the playoff, making it 13 starts without a win despite four runner-up finishes and eight in the top five. He said he hit his correct line, but the greens were firmer than he expected after the restart.

This wasn’t Scheffler’s day, though. It belonged to Hovland, the 28-year-old fan favorite who three years ago made it a race with Scheffler to claim the title of best player in the world. In the time since, Hovland has tinkered with his swing, played erratic golf and, at his lowest point, fallen outside the world’s top 30.

The thing about Hovland is that when he’s at his best, he’s a supernova. And he seems to be rediscovering some of his form. He finished solo third two weeks ago at the Canadian Open, and this week at TPC River Highlands he birdied three holes in a row on the back nine to ultimately send the tournament to a playoff. Before Scheffler missed his putt, Hovland made one from shy of 10 feet to earn his eighth PGA Tour victory.

It is Hovland’s first win since the Valspar Championship in March 2025, and the first Monday playoff on the PGA Tour since Rory McIlroy beat J.J. Spaun to win the 2025 Players Championship.

But back to Scheffler.

Because Scheffler won 13 times over the previous two years, it feels like something is drastically wrong with his 2026 season, which features one win (January’s The American Express) to date. Yet there remains nobody even remotely close to Scheffler’s place as the game’s best player in any ranking. His worst weeks are T22 and T24. He finished runner-up at the Masters and played in the final group at the U.S. Open.

By anyone else’s metrics, he is having an unbelievable season. But by his own analysis, he lacks the “sharpness” required to win. Scheffler’s baseline will almost always put him near the top of leaderboards, because he is just that good. But his iron play — still No. 1 in the world(!) — is nearly half of his normal strokes gained. While he has gone from a poor putter to one of the best on tour, he is still missing many of those putts inside 5 feet that can cost players a win.

In many ways, it feels like Tiger Woods’ 2001 “slump.” He was in the midst of completing the “Tiger Slam” with four major championship wins in a row, but when he went seven tournaments without a win, it led to constant questions and articles. By the time he won that March, a tired Woods joked, “It means my slump is over.” He also said those writers clearly didn’t understand golf.

Golf is a fickle game, and it’s won by the finest of margins. Scheffler will still be the heavy favorite next month at Royal Birkdale for the Open Championship. He is still playing better golf than just about anyone.

He is just not completing those final details. Monday morning was an unfortunate example.
